job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Omar Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my family's textile wholesale shop by eight. We sell fabric and uniforms to schools and tailors in Southgate, and I handle the stock list and the supplier emails. I use AI for most of it now, it writes my orders and spots slow-moving stock. After lunch I send job applications, and in the evening I'm back at the shop. I live with my parents, my uncle Imran and my grandfather.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Business management, with a good result. I did six weeks in the purchasing department of a trading company, comparing supplier quotes and chasing late deliveries. My final project was a plan to cut our shop's unsold stock by a fifth, and I'm actually running it now. It's worked so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the loud claims were never going to be true. I'd tell my uncle Imran that the tools I already use do real work, so keep using them. Online I'd post a few shop tips, because customers like seeing how we do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the world stays the world and the plan stays the plan. I still want a proper job first, where I learn how a big firm buys and sells, and then bring that back to the family shop. A bit of routine purchasing gets automated, but I'd be the one running the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the stock project and aim to show a 20 percent cut in unsold stock by spring. I'd send a dozen applications a week to firms in purchasing and supply chain. I'd also ask the trading company's manager, Mr Bashir, if they could use a junior on contract. And I'd keep putting my wage from the shop into a savings pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Light. I'm eager to start, not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a big firm first, if the family shop needs you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why a big firm first, if the family shop needs you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the stock project show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my father says you can't run a shop well until you've seen a better one. I want to learn how real purchasing works, with proper systems, then come back and do it better. And I want to earn my place, so no one says I only got it because of the name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where businesses split into the ones who adapt and the ones who don't. I'd tell my uncle we should move the shop's ordering and stock onto tools now, while we have time. I'd tell the school customers we can offer faster, cheaper service as a result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm slightly nervous about the entry jobs. Purchasing, comparing quotes and chasing orders are the things software does well, and the trading company might hire fewer juniors. But a shop owner who can use the tools is in a better place than a big firm that's slow to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more of the shop on automated ordering, and use the savings to offer lower prices to schools. I'd also apply for jobs in supply chain tech, where I'd be on the side that builds or runs the tools. And I'd start a small online store for the shop, so we're not tied to local customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, and interested. It's like the market suddenly opened a new road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family shop stay open if you got a job elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would the family shop stay if you got a job elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you offer the schools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but it'd need a plan. My uncle Imran would run the counter, and I'd keep the ordering system running from my phone. A shop is more resilient if it doesn't depend on one person, and I'd set it up that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to move at once, and that regulation should be light but fast. I'd tell customers and neighbours to look after their jobs and savings. I'd say small shops like ours need to be allowed to use the tools freely, or only the big players win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy. A degree in business management would be worth far less, since the thinking jobs go first, and the trading company might not hire anyone. But our shop has hands in it, boxes, deliveries and customers, so it holds out longer than an office would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into the shop. I'd automate everything I can, add an online store, and look for new customers, like tailors in the next town. I'd save more and cut my own spending. I'd also try to get two other small shop owners to share a delivery van, so costs go down. And I'd look for part-time work in logistics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also driven. When there's a big change, I'd rather be the one pushing than the one watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the shop around 2031, when robots can do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens to the shop in 2031 when robots do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the shared delivery van work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the boxes and deliveries start to change, and we'd have to change too. That's three years after the thinking work goes, so I'd have time to get the shop's data, customers and brand in good shape. A shop people trust still counts, even with a robot in the stockroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time for small businesses that move now. I'd tell neighbours to start learning the tools, one hour a week. And I'd say the government should help with apprenticeships, so young people learn on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine. In the next year I'd get a job in supply chain, learn how a large firm runs, and use the next four years to modernise our shop. The risk is waiting too long, because the best jobs go to people who started early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a purchasing job in the next six months and keep the shop's online side running in the evenings. I'd save a third of my pay. By year three I'd put money into new shop equipment, like a better stock scanner, and in year four I'd take over the buying for the shop. I'd also start a small supplier club for local tailors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, with a bit of pressure. I like having a date to build towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a supplier club do for local tailors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would a supplier club do for local tailors?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pick your first employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd order together, so they'd get better prices from the mills. A single tailor orders ten metres, and a group orders a hundred. It costs me some time and gives me a reason for people to stay loyal to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great opportunity, and the family businesses that prepare will do well. I'd tell people to learn the tools, work hard, and keep the community close. I'd also say the government should keep taxes low and let small firms grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm excited. In ten years I could be running a bigger shop, maybe with a second branch, and my job experience would help. I do wonder about the last three years, when the robots show up, but there's time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in the next year, work four or five years in purchasing, then come back to the shop full time at about 28 and open a second branch. I'd invest in equipment gradually, and I'd train two apprentices from local families. I'd also keep saving, because you can't plan growth without a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong and happy. This is the picture I'd have drawn for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprentices learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would the apprentices learn?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at the second branch compared with the first shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to count stock, deal with customers and use the ordering tools. I'd show them how we saved a fifth of our unsold stock and why. A boy or girl who learns that at 18 could run a shop at 25, and I'd be glad to see that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because even a shop with hands in it needs time to change, and two years leaves no room for slow people or slow governments. What would help is light, quick rules, cheap loans for small shops to buy tools, and apprenticeships that start at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more optimistic than most, and I know it comes from having a family business behind me. I'd like other young people to get the same chance to build something of their own.

headlineQuote: I'm more optimistic than most, and I know it comes from having a family business behind me.
portrait: Omar is 23, a business management graduate in Southgate, working in his family's **textile wholesale shop** while he applies for jobs.
He uses AI daily and is running a project to cut the shop's **unsold stock** by a fifth.
His traditional, free-market views favour apprenticeships, light rules and family businesses.
He treats change as a market opening and plans a purchasing job, then a **return to the shop**.
He is calm when time is long and uneasy when it is short, but always driven to act.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, since even a shop needs time to change.
whatWouldHelp: Light, quick **rules** and cheap loans for small shops to buy tools.
